title: Six questions
hookLine: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the questions under every tradition

cards: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" That line is a question. It sits in the eighth Psalm, in a book of prayers and songs, asked while looking up at the night sky.
The old books do this: in the middle of the teaching, the text turns around and asks. Year three starts right there. Not with answers.
With six questions the texts themselves ask, the ones we'll carry to each tradition this year.

teach.b: First, the texts ask, too. It's easy to treat scripture and old philosophy as a place to look things up, but listen to how often they speak in questions.
Second, suffering and death, and the book of Job asks both. Job, sitting in the ashes, says: "Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul?"
Later in the book: "If a man die, shall he live again?"
Third, love, work and forgiveness. In Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet, a woman named Almitra stands up and says, "Speak to us of Love." She doesn't ask whether love matters.
She asks to hear about it.
On work, the Teacher in Ecclesiastes asks, "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?"
And in Matthew's Gospel, Peter brings Jesus a question with a number in it: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
Fourth, awe, which takes us back to the eighth Psalm: what is man, that thou art mindful of him? That's the sixth question, and the last block of the year.
Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe, each with its own long stretch of days, in that order.
Across them we'll hear the Buddha and Job, the Gospels and Rumi, the Stoics, poets and scientists, each in its own voice. Nobody hands you an answer key.
The questions come first, because an answer only means something once you know what it's answering.

how: People who read across traditions often keep a running list of their own big questions and return to the same texts with them over the years, reading for what each text asks as well as what it answers.

games.q: you're Peter. you want to know how far forgiveness has to go. what do you ask?
o: "how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
games.why: Matthew 18:21: Peter's question has a number in it, seven. the answer comes in forgiveness season, much later this year.

practice: Take whichever of today's lines stayed with you: if a man die, shall he live again; how oft shall I forgive; what is man. Say it slowly inside, as a question put to you rather than a quotation.
When an answer jumps up, set it down and ask again, letting the question stand open the way the verse leaves it.
